question.text: Does increased nerve length within the treatment volume improve trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery?
question.context: To test the hypothesis that increasing the nerve length within the treatment volume for trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery would improve pain relief. Eighty-seven patients with typical trigeminal neuralgia were randomized to undergo retrogasserian gamma knife radiosurgery (75 Gy maximal dose with 4-mm diameter collimators) using either one (n = 44) or two (n = 43) isocenters. The median follow-up was 26 months (range 1-36). Pain relief was complete in 57 patients (45 without medication and 12 with low-dose medication), partial in 15, and minimal in another 15 patients. The actuarial rate of obtaining complete pain relief (with or without medication) was 67.7% +/- 5.1%. The pain relief was identical for one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery. Pain relapsed in 30 of 72 responding patients. Facial numbness and mild and severe paresthesias developed in 8, 5, and 1 two-isocenter patients vs. 3, 4, and 0 one-isocenter patients, respectively (p = 0.23). Improved pain relief correlated with younger age (p = 0.025) and fewer prior procedures (p = 0.039) and complications (numbness or paresthesias) correlated with the nerve length irradiated (p = 0.018).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that pain relief was identical between one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery. This indicates that increasing nerve length within the treatment volume does not improve pain relief in trigeminal neuralgia.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Pain relief was identical for one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study mentions facial numbness and paresthesias, these side effects correlated with nerve length irradiated, suggesting they are a consequence of the treatment, not a benefit. The lack of difference in pain relief between the two groups makes the hypothesis of improved pain relief with increased nerve length unlikely.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in pain relief between one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery. The data shows identical pain relief rates (67.7% +/- 5.1%) for both treatment approaches, and complications like numbness and paresthesias were not significantly correlated with nerve length irradiated (p = 0.018). The improved pain relief was more strongly associated with younger age and fewer prior procedures than with nerve length.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The actuarial rate of complete pain relief was identical for both treatment approaches (67.7% +/- 5.1%), indicating that increasing nerve length within the treatment volume did not improve outcomes.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No other factors were found to significantly influence pain relief outcomes. Age and prior procedures were more important predictors than nerve length, suggesting that the hypothesis about nerve length may not be the primary determinant of treatment success.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no difference in pain relief outcomes between one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery, despite the two-isocenter approach increasing nerve length within the treatment volume. Pain relief rates were identical, and while complications correlated with increased nerve length, this did not translate to improved efficacy.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Pain relief was identical for one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery, indicating that increasing nerve length did not improve therapeutic outcomes.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether increased nerve length might improve efficacy, but the data show no difference in pain relief, ruling out this hypothesis.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: Based on the clinical case, increasing the nerve length within the treatment volume for trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery does improve pain relief. This is supported by the actuarial rate of obtaining complete pain relief which was 67.7% +/- 5.1% and the correlation of improved pain relief with younger age and fewer prior procedures. Additionally, complications such as numbness or paresthesias correlated with the nerve length irradiated, indicating that targeting a longer nerve length may reduce the incidence of these side effects.
openbio_8b.critical_evidence: The actuarial rate of obtaining complete pain relief (with or without medication) was 67.7% +/- 5.1%
openbio_8b.differential_considered: None of the options provided were considered differentials as the clinical case clearly supports the positive outcome of increasing nerve length within the treatment volume for trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: I considered whether longer irradiated nerve might reduce nerve damage or improve neural tissue tolerance, but the randomized trial’s results and lack of statistical significance for nerve length suggest that technical adjustments in the volume do not confer a clinical advantage over standard approaches.
